title: In 20 resting flies, the FlyWire sensory hierarchy of 67 brain regions did not predict their activity timescales; apparent effects depended on the estimator and on small, noisy central-complex regions
abstract: Question: in primate cortex, areas higher in the anatomical hierarchy have longer intrinsic timescales. The campaign record tested this in mouse cortex (null), C. elegans (opposite sign when moving) and larval zebrafish (null), but not in the adult fly. Data: resting two-photon GCaMP6s imaging of 20 flies (Turner, Mann and Clandinin 2021, MIT license; 67 Ito atlas regions, 1.2 Hz) and the FlyWire v783 connectome. Primary hierarchy measure (pre-specified): synapse-weighted sensory distance of the neurons that receive input in each neuropil (backward input-weighted walk to sensory neurons). Primary timescale: exponential fit to the autocorrelation (lags 0.8-30 s) of the high-pass filtered region signal. Results: the primary test was null (Spearman rho 0.07, fly-bootstrap 95% CI -0.22 to 0.32, spatial-surrogate p 0.54; 11 of 20 flies with rho > 0). Other estimators gave different signs: linear detrend rho +0.37, global-signal regression -0.26, integral timescale -0.31. Spectra were consistent over flies: higher regions had less 25-100 s power (rho -0.46, 0 of 20 flies > 0) and more 1.7-7 s power (rho +0.45). But higher regions are smaller (rho -0.31 with voxel count) and small regions are noisier (rho -0.75); with size and brightness control and without the central complex, no relation remained (all |partial rho| <= 0.21). Hemibrain region trophic level gave rho 0.03 (p 0.89). In 368 hemibrain supervoxels a weak positive trend (rho 0.23, spatial p 0.064) was absent inside parent regions (rho 0.06). Conclusion: no evidence that higher fly regions have longer timescales. Limitations: region-mean pan-neuronal signals, no behaviour data, low reliability of the primary map (split-half 0.31), size confound, connectome and activity from different flies.

display.caption: Region activity timescale (median over 20 flies, log scale) against FlyWire sensory distance of inputs (L_in) for 67 regions. A: pre-specified primary estimator (high-pass 0.01 Hz, exponential fit), no relation. B: after global-signal regression, a weak negative relation. C: single-fly rho for the primary test (11 of 20 above zero).

A: Spearman rho between L_in and relative band power, raw and with the white-noise floor removed; labels give the number of flies with rho > 0. B: regions high in the hierarchy (central complex) are small. C: small regions have a larger white-noise share of power, which can produce apparent fast dynamics.

Raw (open) and partial (filled; control for log voxel count and log mean fluorescence) Spearman rho with L_in for timescale and spectral measures, for all 67 regions and for 59 regions without the central complex. No partial relation remains without the central complex.
